questions.question: Describe the founding and organisation of the Asante kingdom.
questions.expected_answer: The Asante are an Akan people of the forest region of central Ghana who were tributaries of Denkyira in the seventeenth century. Around 1700 Osei Tutu of Kumasi united several chiefdoms with the priest Okomfo Anokye, who according to tradition brought down the Golden Stool, believed to hold the spirit of the nation; chiefs buried their own stools and swore loyalty to it and to Osei Tutu as Asantehene, and no one sat on it. The Asante defeated Denkyira around 1701 at Feyiase and expanded under rulers such as Opoku Ware over most of modern Ghana. The Asantehene ruled with a council of senior chiefs and a national assembly; the queen mother advised and helped choose kings; a bureaucracy in Kumasi managed taxes, trade, roads and diplomacy, using Muslim scribes; great roads radiated from Kumasi; the army was large, disciplined and organised in divisions with firearms. Kumasi was a planned city, with goldsmiths, kente weavers, gold weights and festivals such as Odwira.

questions.question: Explain the sources of Asante wealth and describe trade and the role of European forts on the Gold Coast.
questions.expected_answer: Asante wealth came from gold, mined and panned in the forest; gold dust was currency and large nuggets belonged to the state. Kola nuts were traded north to savanna and Sahel markets for cloth, salt, livestock and leather, linked to trans-Saharan routes, while trade went south to Europeans on the coast. The Portuguese built Elmina in 1482, giving the name Gold Coast; the Dutch took it in 1637, and the English, Danes, Swedes and Germans built forts, with Cape Coast Castle the main British base, more forts than anywhere else in Africa. Europeans paid rent to coastal rulers and relied on African middlemen such as the Fante, which caused Asante-Fante conflict. In the eighteenth century the slave trade dominated; the Asante sold captives, often taken in war, for firearms, gunpowder, cloth, metal goods and alcohol, and enslaved people were held in fort dungeons. After Britain abolished the trade in 1807, the Asante shifted to exporting gold, kola and ivory.

questions.question: Describe relations between the Asante and the British in the early nineteenth century and evaluate the sources historians use.
questions.expected_answer: The British wanted to expand inland trade, protect their Fante allies and end the slave trade; the Asante wanted control of trade and of the coastal states. Bowdich's mission of 1817 found Kumasi large, orderly and wealthy and made a treaty, and Dupuis visited in 1820. The Asante treated Europeans as rivals and partners, received and sent envoys, and educated princes such as Owusu Ansa in England. In January 1824 the Asante defeated Governor MacCarthy at Nsamankow, killing him, but in 1826 the British and allies won at Katamanso near Accra, and a treaty in 1831 recognised the coastal states' independence from Asante, leaving an uneasy balance for forty years. Sources include Asante oral traditions, which preserve the Asante view but may contain symbolic elements and favour the royal family; European accounts, which give eyewitness detail but misunderstand customs and serve European aims; Arabic documents, company records, archaeology and objects. Combined, they give a fuller picture.
